tname: Operations with numbers in the form a × 10^k
text:
(a) Write $0.000\,047\,2$ in the form $a\times10^{k}$, where $1\le a<10$ and $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. [1]

(b) Find the value of
$$\frac{(6\times10^{5})\times(4\times10^{-2})}{8\times10^{-3}}$$
giving your answer in the form $a\times10^{k}$, where $1\le a<10$ and $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. [3]
ms:
**(a)** $4.72\times10^{-5}$ A1 [1]

**(b)** numerator: $(6\times4)\times10^{5-2}=24\times10^{3}$ $(=2.4\times10^{4})$ (M1)(A1)

$\dfrac{24\times10^{3}}{8\times10^{-3}}=3\times10^{6}$ A1

*Award (M1) for correctly combining powers of 10 in either the numerator or the division. Accept equivalent working with 2.4×10⁴. Do not award the final A1 for $3\,000\,000$ (not in the required form).* [3]

tname: Operations with numbers in the form a × 10^k
text:
The mean distance from the Earth to the Sun is $1.496\times10^{8}$ km. The speed of light is $2.998\times10^{5}\ \text{km s}^{-1}$.

(a) Calculate the time, in seconds, that light takes to travel from the Sun to the Earth. Give your answer in the form $a\times10^{k}$, where $1\le a<10$ and $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. [2]

A light-year is the distance light travels in $365.25$ days.

(b) Show that one light-year is $9.46\times10^{12}$ km, correct to three significant figures. [2]

The distance from the Earth to the star Proxima Centauri is approximately $4.02\times10^{13}$ km.

(c) Find the distance from the Earth to Proxima Centauri in light-years. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $\dfrac{1.496\times10^{8}}{2.998\times10^{5}}$ (M1)

$=499\ \text{s}=4.99\times10^{2}\ \text{s}$ A1

*Accept $4.990\times10^{2}$.* [2]

**(b)** $365.25\times24\times60\times60\ (=31\,557\,600\ \text{s})$ M1

$2.998\times10^{5}\times31\,557\,600=9.46097\ldots\times10^{12}$ A1

$=9.46\times10^{12}$ km AG

*The unrounded value must be seen for A1.* [2]

**(c)** $\dfrac{4.02\times10^{13}}{9.46\times10^{12}}$ (M1)

$=4.25$ light-years A1

*Accept 4.249… Using the unrounded light-year also gives 4.25.* [2]

tname: Operations with numbers in the form a × 10^k
text:
In this question, use the following values.

| | mass (kg) |
|---|---|
| hydrogen atom | $1.67\times10^{-27}$ |
| Moon | $7.35\times10^{22}$ |
| Earth | $5.972\times10^{24}$ |
| Sun | $1.989\times10^{30}$ |

(a) Assuming the Sun were made entirely of hydrogen atoms, estimate the number of hydrogen atoms in the Sun. Give your answer in the form $a\times10^{k}$, where $1\le a<10$ and $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. [2]

(b) Find how many times greater the mass of the Sun is than the mass of the Earth. [2]

(c) Find the total mass of the Earth and the Moon. Give your answer in the form $a\times10^{k}$, where $1\le a<10$ and $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. [2]

Matchsticks are used to make a sequence of patterns. The first three patterns are shown.

![Patterns 1, 2 and 3 made of 1, 2 and 3 squares of matchsticks in a row](qbank/img/gen_math_SL1.2_1.svg)

Pattern 1 uses 4 matchsticks, pattern 2 uses 7 matchsticks and pattern 3 uses 10 matchsticks. The numbers of matchsticks form an arithmetic sequence.

(a) Find the number of matchsticks in pattern 20. [2]

(b) Find the total number of matchsticks needed to make all of the patterns from pattern 1 to pattern 20. [2]

(c) One pattern uses exactly 151 matchsticks. Find which pattern this is. [2]

The first eight terms of an arithmetic sequence $u_1,u_2,u_3,\ldots$ are plotted on the graph below.

![Points (n, u_n) for n = 1 to 8 lying on a straight line, from (1, 3) to (8, 31)](qbank/img/gen_math_SL1.2_2.svg)

(a) Write down the value of $u_1$ and the value of the common difference $d$. [2]

(b) Show that the sum of the first $n$ terms is $S_n=2n^{2}+n$. [2]

(c) Find the value of $n$ for which $S_n=465$. [2]

(d) Determine whether $2026$ is a term of this sequence. Justify your answer. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $u_1=3$ A1

$d=4$ A1 [2]

**(b)** $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2\times3+(n-1)\times4\right)$ M1

$=\dfrac{n}{2}(4n+2)$ A1

$=2n^{2}+n$ AG

*Award M1A0 if the step before the AG line is not seen.* [2]

**(c)** $2n^{2}+n=465$ (M1)

$n=15$ A1

*Award A0 if $n=-15.5$ is also given as a final answer.* [2]

**(d)** $u_n=4n-1$; $4n-1=2026\Rightarrow n=506.75$ M1

$n$ is not an integer, so 2026 is not a term of the sequence R1

*Alternative: all terms are odd ($4n-1$), 2026 is even, so not a term. Award R1 only if supported by working (M1).* [2]

text:
A theatre has 30 rows of seats. There are 22 seats in the first row and each row has 3 more seats than the row in front of it.

(a) Find the number of seats in the last row. [2]

(b) Find the total number of seats in the theatre. [2]

For a performance, the seats are filled starting at the front row, and each row is completely filled before people sit in the next row.

(c) Find the least number of rows needed to seat 1000 people. [3]
ms:
**(a)** $u_{30}=22+29\times3$ (M1)

$=109$ A1 [2]

**(b)** $S_{30}=\dfrac{30}{2}(22+109)$ (M1)

$=1965$ A1

*FT from (a).* [2]

**(c)** $\dfrac{n}{2}\left(2\times22+3(n-1)\right)\ge1000$ (M1)

*Accept an equation, or a table of values with $S_{19}=931$ and $S_{20}=1010$.*

$n=19.87\ldots$ (A1)

20 rows A1

*Do not award the final A1 for 19.9 or 19.* [3]

text:
Maria opens a savings account and deposits €50 in the first month. Each month after that she deposits €8 more than in the previous month. No interest is paid.

(a) Find the amount Maria deposits in the 12th month. [2]

(b) Find the total amount Maria has deposited after 12 months. [2]

(c) Show that the total amount, in euros, that Maria has deposited after $n$ months is $4n^{2}+46n$. [2]

Jon opens a savings account at the same time with an initial deposit of €300, and then deposits €120 at the end of every month. After $n$ months Jon has deposited a total of $300+120n$ euros.

(d) Find the first month in which Maria's total deposits exceed Jon's total deposits. [3]

(e) Maria wants her total deposits to reach at least €5000.

 (i) Find the least number of months needed.

 (ii) Find how much more Maria will have deposited than Jon at the end of this month. [4]

(a) Find the sum of all the positive integers less than 500 that are multiples of 6. [4]

(b) Hence find the sum of all the positive integers less than or equal to 500 that are **not** multiples of 6. [2]

(a) Find the value of $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{40}(3r-5)$. [3]

(b) Given that $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{k}(3r-5)=1245$, find the value of $k$. [3]
ms:
**(a)** first term $-2$, last term $115$, 40 terms (A1)

$S_{40}=\dfrac{40}{2}(-2+115)$ (M1)

$=2260$ A1 [3]

**(b)** $\dfrac{k}{2}\left(-4+3(k-1)\right)=1245\Rightarrow\dfrac{k(3k-7)}{2}=1245$ M1

$3k^{2}-7k-2490=0$ A1

$(k-30)(3k+83)=0\Rightarrow k=30$ (reject negative/non-integer root) A1 [3]

text:
The diagram shows the first three stages of a pattern. At stage 1 there is one shaded equilateral triangle with side 16 cm. To make each new stage, every shaded triangle is divided into four equal equilateral triangles and the middle one is removed (left unshaded).

![Stages 1 to 3: one shaded triangle; then three shaded triangles with the middle removed; then nine shaded triangles](qbank/img/gen_math_SL1.3_1.svg)

(a) Find the number of shaded triangles at stage 5. [2]

(b) Find the side length of each shaded triangle at stage 5. [2]

Let $A$ be the area of the shaded triangle at stage 1.

(c) Show that the total shaded area at stage $n$ is $\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^{n-1}A$. [2]
ms:
**(a)** numbers of triangles $1,3,9,\ldots$: geometric with $r=3$ (M1)

$u_5=1\times3^{4}=81$ A1 [2]

**(b)** side lengths $16,8,4,\ldots$: geometric with $r=\dfrac12$ (M1)

$16\times\left(\dfrac12\right)^{4}=1$ cm A1 [2]

**(c)** each stage keeps 3 of the 4 equal smaller triangles, so the shaded area is multiplied by $\dfrac34$ R1

areas $A,\ \dfrac34A,\ \left(\dfrac34\right)^{2}A,\ldots$ is geometric with $u_1=A$, $r=\dfrac34$, so $u_n=\left(\dfrac34\right)^{n-1}A$ A1AG

*Alternative: $3^{n-1}$ triangles each of area $\left(\frac14\right)^{n-1}A$ (side halved, area quartered) M1A1.* [2]

text:
In a geometric sequence, $u_2=12$ and $u_5=-96$.

(a) Find the common ratio. [3]

(b) Find $u_1$. [1]

(c) Find the sum of the first 8 terms. [2]

(a) Show that $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}4\left(3^{r-1}\right)=2\left(3^{n}-1\right)$. [2]

(b) Find the least value of $n$ for which $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}4\left(3^{r-1}\right)>10^{6}$. [3]

An arithmetic sequence has first term $a$ and common difference $d$, where $a\ne0$ and $d\ne0$. The first, third and ninth terms of this arithmetic sequence, $u_1$, $u_3$ and $u_9$, are the first three terms of a geometric sequence.

(a) Show that $d=a$. [3]

(b) Find the common ratio of the geometric sequence. [2]

It is now given that $a=5$.

(c) Find the sum of the first 20 terms of the arithmetic sequence. [2]

(d) Find the least number of terms of the geometric sequence whose sum exceeds $100\,000$. [3]

(e) Show that every term of the geometric sequence is also a term of the arithmetic sequence. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $u_3=a+2d$, $u_9=a+8d$ (A1)

$(a+2d)^{2}=a(a+8d)$ or $\dfrac{a+2d}{a}=\dfrac{a+8d}{a+2d}$ M1

$a^{2}+4ad+4d^{2}=a^{2}+8ad\Rightarrow4d^{2}=4ad$ A1

$d\ne0\Rightarrow d=a$ AG [3]

**(b)** $r=\dfrac{a+2d}{a}=\dfrac{3a}{a}$ (M1)

$r=3$ A1 [2]

**(c)** $S_{20}=\dfrac{20}{2}\left(2\times5+19\times5\right)$ (M1)

$=1050$ A1 [2]

**(d)** $\dfrac{5(3^{n}-1)}{3-1}>100\,000$ M1

$3^{n}>40\,001$ A1

$3^{9}=19\,683<40\,001<59\,049=3^{10}$, so $n=10$ A1

*FT from their $r$.* [3]

**(e)** $k$th term of geometric sequence is $5\times3^{k-1}$; $m$th term of arithmetic sequence is $5+5(m-1)=5m$ M1

$5\times3^{k-1}=5m$ with $m=3^{k-1}$, a positive integer, so it is the $\left(3^{k-1}\right)$th term of the arithmetic sequence R1

*Award R1 only if the integer nature of $3^{k-1}$ is stated or clearly implied.* [2]

text:
A ball is dropped from a height of 10 m onto horizontal ground. After each bounce it rises to 80% of the height from which it last fell.

![Path of a ball dropped from 10 m, rising to 8 m after the first bounce, then lower each time](qbank/img/gen_math_SL1.3_5.svg)

(a) Find the maximum height reached by the ball after its 4th bounce. [2]

(b) Find the total vertical distance the ball has travelled when it hits the ground for the 6th time. [3]

(c) Find the number of the first bounce after which the ball rises to a height of less than 1 m. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $10\times0.8^{4}$ (M1)

$=4.10$ m $(4.096)$ A1 [2]

**(b)** heights of bounces 1 to 5: $8,6.4,5.12,4.096,3.2768$ (sum $=26.8928$) (M1)

$10+2\times\dfrac{8(1-0.8^{5})}{1-0.8}$ M1

$=63.8$ m $(63.7856)$ A1

*Award M1 for doubling the bounce heights and adding the initial 10 m. Award M1M0A0 for $10+8+\cdots$ without doubling.* [3]

**(c)** $10\times0.8^{n}<1$ (M1)

$n>10.3\ldots$, so the 11th bounce A1 [2]

text:
Kai is training for a cycling event. On day 1 he cycles 20 km. Each day after that he cycles 10% further than on the previous day.

(a) Find the distance Kai cycles on day 8. [2]

(b) Find the total distance Kai cycles in the first 8 days. [2]

(c) Find the least number of days for which the total distance Kai has cycled is more than 500 km. [3]

tname: Financial applications: compound interest and depreciation
text:
Lena invests €5000 in an account that pays a nominal annual interest rate of 3.5%, compounded annually.

(a) Find the value of Lena's investment after 8 years. Give your answer correct to two decimal places. [3]

(b) Find the interest Lena earns over the 8 years. [1]
ms:
**(a)** $5000\left(1+\dfrac{3.5}{100}\right)^{8}$ (M1)(A1)

*Award (M1) for substitution into the compound interest formula, (A1) for correct substitution. Or for GDC TVM: N = 8, I% = 3.5, PV = −5000, PMT = 0, P/Y = C/Y = 1.*

€6584.05 A1 [3]

**(b)** $6584.05-5000=$ €1584.05 A1

*FT from (a).* [1]

tname: Financial applications: compound interest and depreciation
text:
Ravi invests €12 000 in an account paying a nominal annual interest rate of 4.2%, compounded monthly.

(a) Find the value of the investment after 5 years. Give your answer correct to two decimal places. [3]

(b) Find the number of complete years after which the value of the investment first exceeds €18 000. [3]

tname: Financial applications: compound interest and depreciation
text:
A new car costs €32 000. Its value depreciates by 18% each year.

(a) Find the value of the car after 4 years. [2]

(b) Find the number of complete years after which the value of the car first falls below €10 000. [3]

A second car, also bought for €32 000, depreciates at a constant annual rate of $r\%$. Its value after 4 years is €15 000.

(c) Find the value of $r$. [2]

tname: Financial applications: compound interest and depreciation
text:
The value, $V$ euros, of a machine $t$ years after it was bought is modelled by $V=V_0\left(1-\dfrac{r}{100}\right)^{t}$, where $r\%$ is the constant annual rate of depreciation. The graph of $V$ against $t$ passes through the points $(0,\ 50\,000)$ and $(3,\ 25\,600)$.

![Decreasing exponential curve of V against t through (0, 50 000) and (3, 25 600)](qbank/img/gen_math_SL1.4_4.svg)

(a) Find the annual rate of depreciation, $r\%$. [3]

(b) Find the value of the machine 6 years after it was bought. [2]

tname: Financial applications: compound interest and depreciation
text:
Ana has €20 000 to invest for 10 years. She considers two options.

- Option A: a nominal annual interest rate of 5%, compounded annually.
- Option B: a nominal annual interest rate of 4.8%, compounded monthly.

(a) Find the value of Ana's investment after 10 years under

 (i) Option A;

 (ii) Option B. [4]

(b) Hence state which option Ana should choose. [1]

Ana chooses Option A. Over the 10 years, prices are expected to rise by 2.5% per year, compounded annually.

(c) Find the value of Ana's investment after 10 years in terms of today's prices, by dividing its final value by the factor by which prices will have increased over the 10 years. [2]

Ana's friend Bruno also invests €20 000 for 10 years, with interest compounded quarterly at a nominal annual rate of $k\%$. The value of his investment after 10 years is €35 000.

(d) Find the value of $k$. [3]

(e) For Option A, find the least number of complete years needed for the value of the investment to be at least three times the amount invested. [3]
ms:
**(a)(i)** $20\,000(1.05)^{10}$ (M1)

€32 577.89 A1

**(ii)** $20\,000\left(1+\dfrac{0.048}{12}\right)^{120}$ (M1)

€32 290.56 A1

*Accept TVM entries with the correct N, I%, PV and C/Y. Accept answers to 3 s.f. (€32 600, €32 300).* [4]

**(b)** Option A (it gives the greater final value) A1

*FT from (a).* [1]

**(c)** price factor $1.025^{10}$ $(=1.2800\ldots)$; $\dfrac{32\,577.89}{1.025^{10}}$ (M1)

€25 449.80 A1

*Accept €25 400 (3 s.f.). FT from (a)(i). Award M1A0 for €25 601.69 (using a 2.5% "real" interest rate, which is not the method asked for).* [2]

**(d)** $20\,000\left(1+\dfrac{k}{400}\right)^{40}=35\,000$ (M1)(A1)

$k=5.64$ $(5.6354\ldots)$ A1 [3]

**(e)** $20\,000(1.05)^{n}\ge60\,000$ (M1)

$n\ge22.5\ldots$ (A1)

23 years A1 [3]

text:
(a) Solve the equation $3^{x+1}=40$. [2]

The population, $P$, of a town $t$ years after 1 January 2020 is modelled by $P=1200\,\mathrm{e}^{0.035t}$.

(b) Find the time, in years, after which the population first reaches 2000. [3]

Solve each of the following equations, giving your answers in exact form.

(a) $\mathrm{e}^{2x}=9$ [2]

(b) $\ln(x-2)=3$ [2]

(c) $3\times10^{x-1}=12$ [2]

The graph of $y=f(x)$, where $f(x)=a\times b^{x}$ with $a>0$, $b>0$, passes through the points $(0,\ 5)$ and $(3,\ 40)$.

![Increasing exponential curve through the points (0, 5) and (3, 40)](qbank/img/gen_math_SL1.5_4.svg)

(a) Find the value of $a$ and the value of $b$. [3]

(b) Find the value of $x$ for which $f(x)=100$. [2]
Prove that $(n+3)^{2}-(n-3)^{2}$ is a multiple of 12 for all integers $n$. [3]
ms:
$(n^{2}+6n+9)-(n^{2}-6n+9)$ M1

$=12n$ A1

$n$ is an integer, so $12n$ is a multiple of 12 R1

*Alternative: difference of two squares $\left((n+3)+(n-3)\right)\left((n+3)-(n-3)\right)=(2n)(6)$ M1A1, R1 as above. Do not award R1 for checking particular values of $n$; award M0A0R0 for a proof by examples only.* [3]

text:
The diagram shows how square arrays of dots can be built by adding L-shaped layers of dots.

![Square arrays of 1, 4, 9 and 16 dots, each made by adding an L-shaped layer of 1, 3, 5 and 7 dots](qbank/img/gen_math_SL1.6_2.svg)

(a) Prove that the sum of the first $n$ odd positive integers is $n^{2}$. [3]

(b) Hence show that the sum of all the odd integers from $2n+1$ to $4n-1$ inclusive is $3n^{2}$. [3]
ms:
**(a)** the odd numbers $1,3,5,\ldots$ form an arithmetic sequence with $u_1=1$, $d=2$; the $n$th odd number is $2n-1$ M1

$S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\left(1+(2n-1)\right)$ A1

$=\dfrac{n}{2}(2n)=n^{2}$ A1AG

*A purely diagrammatic argument without algebra earns at most M1.* [3]

**(b)** $2n+1$ is the $(n+1)$th odd number and $4n-1$ is the $(2n)$th odd number R1

required sum $=(\text{sum of first }2n\text{ odd numbers})-(\text{sum of first }n\text{ odd numbers})=(2n)^{2}-n^{2}$ M1

$=4n^{2}-n^{2}=3n^{2}$ A1AG

*Alternative: arithmetic series with $n$ terms, first term $2n+1$, last term $4n-1$: $\frac{n}{2}(6n)=3n^{2}$; award R1 for the number of terms, M1A1.* [3]

text:
(a) Prove that the sum of the squares of any two consecutive integers is odd. [3]

(b) Prove that the square of any odd integer is one more than a multiple of 8. [4]
ms:
**(a)** let the integers be $n$ and $n+1$:

$n^{2}+(n+1)^{2}=2n^{2}+2n+1$ M1A1

$=2(n^{2}+n)+1$, where $n^{2}+n$ is an integer, so the sum is odd R1 [3]

**(b)** let the odd integer be $2k+1$, $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ M1

$(2k+1)^{2}=4k^{2}+4k+1=4k(k+1)+1$ A1

$k$ and $k+1$ are consecutive integers so one of them is even, hence $k(k+1)=2m$ for some integer $m$ R1

$(2k+1)^{2}=4(2m)+1=8m+1$, which is one more than a multiple of 8 A1AG

*Do not award the R1 without justification that $k(k+1)$ is even.* [4]

text:
(a) Show that $\dfrac{1}{r}-\dfrac{1}{r+1}=\dfrac{1}{r(r+1)}$, for $r\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}$. [2]

(b) Hence show that $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{1}{r(r+1)}=\frac{n}{n+1}$. [3]

(c) Find the least value of $n$ for which $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{1}{r(r+1)}>0.99$. [2]
ms:
**(a)** $\dfrac{1}{r}-\dfrac{1}{r+1}=\dfrac{(r+1)-r}{r(r+1)}$ M1A1

$=\dfrac{1}{r(r+1)}$ AG

*Working from RHS to LHS is also acceptable.* [2]

**(b)** $\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{1}{r(r+1)}=\left(1-\frac12\right)+\left(\frac12-\frac13\right)+\cdots+\left(\frac1n-\frac{1}{n+1}\right)$ M1A1

*M1 for using (a) to write the sum as differences; A1 for at least the first two and last term shown.*

intermediate terms cancel, leaving $1-\dfrac{1}{n+1}=\dfrac{n}{n+1}$ A1AG [3]

**(c)** $\dfrac{n}{n+1}>0.99\Rightarrow n>0.99n+0.99\Rightarrow0.01n>0.99$ (M1)

$n>99$, so $n=100$ A1

*Do not award A1 for $n=99$ (gives exactly 0.99).* [2]

text:
(a) Simplify $\dfrac{(2x^{3})^{4}}{4x^{5}}$. [2]

(b) Write $8^{x}\times4^{x+1}$ in the form $2^{ax+b}$, where $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$. [2]

(c) Hence solve the equation $8^{x}\times4^{x+1}=\dfrac{1}{16}$. [2]

Let $\log_a 2=p$ and $\log_a 3=q$, where $a>1$. Write each of the following in terms of $p$ and $q$.

(a) $\log_a 12$ [2]

(b) $\log_a\left(\dfrac98\right)$ [2]

(c) $\log_a\sqrt{6a}$ [2]
ms:
**(a)** $\log_a(2^{2}\times3)=2\log_a2+\log_a3$ (M1)

$=2p+q$ A1 [2]

**(b)** $\log_a 9-\log_a 8=2\log_a3-3\log_a2$ (M1)

$=2q-3p$ A1 [2]

**(c)** $\dfrac12\left(\log_a2+\log_a3+\log_a a\right)$ (M1)

$=\dfrac12(p+q+1)$ A1

*Accept $\frac{p+q+1}{2}$.* [2]

text: Solve the equation $\log_2(x+3)+\log_2(x-3)=4$. [5]
ms:
$\log_2\left((x+3)(x-3)\right)=4$ M1

$(x+3)(x-3)=2^{4}$ M1

$x^{2}-9=16\Rightarrow x^{2}=25\Rightarrow x=\pm5$ A1

$x=-5$ is rejected since $\log_2(x-3)$ (and $\log_2(x+3)$) is undefined for $x=-5$ R1

$x=5$ A1

*Award the final A1 only if $x=-5$ is rejected. Award R1 for a valid reason for rejecting $-5$.* [5]

text: Solve the equation $2\times4^{x}-9\times2^{x}+4=0$. [5]
ms:
let $y=2^{x}$, so $4^{x}=(2^{2})^{x}=y^{2}$ M1

$2y^{2}-9y+4=0$ A1

$(2y-1)(y-4)=0\Rightarrow y=\dfrac12$ or $y=4$ A1

$2^{x}=\dfrac12\Rightarrow x=-1$; $2^{x}=4\Rightarrow x=2$ A1A1 [5]

text:
(a) Show that $\log_9 x=\dfrac12\log_3 x$, for $x>0$. [2]

(b) Hence solve $\log_3 x+\log_9 x=6$. [3]

(c) Solve $\log_3 x\times\log_9 x=8$. [3]
ms:
**(a)** $\log_9 x=\dfrac{\log_3 x}{\log_3 9}$ M1

$=\dfrac{\log_3 x}{2}$ A1AG

*Alternative: let $\log_9x=y$, so $x=9^{y}=3^{2y}$, hence $\log_3x=2y$ M1A1.* [2]

**(b)** $\log_3 x+\dfrac12\log_3 x=6$ M1

$\dfrac32\log_3x=6\Rightarrow\log_3 x=4$ A1

$x=3^{4}=81$ A1 [3]

**(c)** $\dfrac12(\log_3x)^{2}=8$ M1

$(\log_3x)^{2}=16\Rightarrow\log_3x=\pm4$ A1

$x=81$ or $x=\dfrac{1}{81}$ A1

*Award A0 if only $x=81$ is given.* [3]

text:
The pH of a solution is defined by $\text{pH}=-\log_{10}\left[\text{H}^{+}\right]$, where $\left[\text{H}^{+}\right]$ is the concentration of hydrogen ions in $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$.

(a) Find the pH of a solution with $\left[\text{H}^{+}\right]=3.2\times10^{-4}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$. [2]

(b) Solution X has a pH of 2.5 and solution Y has a pH of 4.1. Find how many times greater the hydrogen ion concentration of solution X is than that of solution Y. [3]

tname: Sum of infinite convergent geometric sequences
text:
The diagram shows a square of side 1 unit. The square is divided into four equal squares and the bottom-left square, A, is shaded. The top-right square is then divided into four equal squares and its bottom-left square, B, is shaded. This process continues indefinitely.

![Unit square with shaded squares A (side 1/2), B (side 1/4) and smaller shaded squares continuing towards the top-right corner](qbank/img/gen_math_SL1.8_1.svg)

(a) Write down the areas of the first three shaded squares and state the common ratio of the resulting geometric sequence. [2]

(b) Find the total shaded area. [2]

(c) Using the sum of an infinite geometric series, write the recurring decimal $0.\overline{72}=0.727272\ldots$ as a fraction in its simplest form. [3]

tname: Sum of infinite convergent geometric sequences
text:
Consider the infinite geometric series
$$1+\frac{2x}{3}+\frac{4x^{2}}{9}+\frac{8x^{3}}{27}+\cdots$$

(a) Find the values of $x$ for which the series converges. [2]

(b) Given that the sum of the series is 4, find the value of $x$. [3]
ms:
**(a)** $r=\dfrac{2x}{3}$; converges when $\left|\dfrac{2x}{3}\right|<1$ (M1)

$-\dfrac32<x<\dfrac32$ A1 [2]

**(b)** $\dfrac{1}{1-\frac{2x}{3}}=4$ M1

$\dfrac{3}{3-2x}=4\Rightarrow3=12-8x$ A1

$x=\dfrac98$ A1

*Final A1 may be withheld if $x$ is outside their interval from (a) and no comment made; $\frac98$ lies within $-\frac32<x<\frac32$.* [3]

tname: Sum of infinite convergent geometric sequences
text:
A square has side 10 cm. A second square is drawn inside it by joining the midpoints of its sides. A third square is drawn by joining the midpoints of the sides of the second square, and this process continues indefinitely.

![A 10 cm square with a sequence of squares inside it, each formed by joining the midpoints of the sides of the previous square](qbank/img/gen_math_SL1.8_3.svg)

(a) Show that the areas of the squares form a geometric sequence with common ratio $\dfrac12$. [2]

(b) Find the sum of the areas of all the squares. [2]

(c) Find the sum of the perimeters of all the squares. [3]
ms:
**(a)** side of second square $=\sqrt{5^{2}+5^{2}}=\sqrt{50}=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt2}$ M1

each side is multiplied by $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ so each area is multiplied by $\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)^{2}=\dfrac12$ (areas $100, 50, 25,\ldots$) R1AG [2]

**(b)** $S_\infty=\dfrac{100}{1-\frac12}$ (M1)

$=200\ \text{cm}^{2}$ A1 [2]

**(c)** perimeters $40,\ \dfrac{40}{\sqrt2},\ 20,\ldots$; $r=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ (A1)

$S_\infty=\dfrac{40}{1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}}$ (M1)

$=137$ cm $(136.568\ldots$, exact $80+40\sqrt2)$ A1 [3]

tname: Sum of infinite convergent geometric sequences
text:
A pendulum is released and swings back and forth. The length of the arc of its first swing is 40 cm. The length of the arc of each swing after that is 92% of the length of the previous swing.

![A pendulum bob swinging from one side to the other along an arc of length 40 cm](qbank/img/gen_math_SL1.8_4.svg)

(a) Find the length of the arc of the 10th swing. [2]

(b) Find the total distance the pendulum bob would travel if it continued swinging indefinitely. [2]

(c) Find the least number of swings after which the total distance travelled by the bob exceeds 450 cm. [3]

tname: Sum of infinite convergent geometric sequences
text:
An infinite geometric sequence has first term $u_1$ and common ratio $r$, where $0<r<1$. The second term is 6 and the sum to infinity is 27.

(a) Show that $9r^{2}-9r+2=0$. [4]

(b) Find the two possible values of $r$. [2]

(c) Find the corresponding values of $u_1$. [2]

For the remainder of this question, consider the sequence with the larger value of $r$.

(d) Find the sum of all the terms of the sequence from the 4th term onwards. [3]

(e) A new sequence is formed by squaring every term of this sequence. Find the sum to infinity of the new sequence. [3]
ms:
**(a)** $u_1r=6$ and $\dfrac{u_1}{1-r}=27$ A1A1

$\dfrac{6}{r(1-r)}=27$ or $6=27r(1-r)$ M1

$27r-27r^{2}=6\Rightarrow27r^{2}-27r+6=0$ A1

$9r^{2}-9r+2=0$ AG [4]

**(b)** $(3r-1)(3r-2)=0$ (M1)

$r=\dfrac13$ or $r=\dfrac23$ A1 [2]

**(c)** $r=\dfrac13\Rightarrow u_1=18$; $r=\dfrac23\Rightarrow u_1=9$ A1A1 [2]

**(d)** $r=\dfrac23$, $u_1=9$: first three terms $9,6,4$, so $S_3=19$ (M1)

required sum $=S_\infty-S_3=27-19$ M1

$=8$ A1

*Alternative: $u_4=\frac83$ and $\dfrac{8/3}{1-2/3}=8$. FT from (b) and (c).* [3]

**(e)** new sequence $81,36,16,\ldots$: geometric with first term $81$ and ratio $\dfrac49$ (A1)

$\dfrac{81}{1-\frac49}$ M1

$=\dfrac{729}{5}$ $(=145.8)$ A1 [3]

text: Expand $(2+x)^{4}$ in ascending powers of $x$, simplifying each term. [4]
ms:
use of binomial expansion or Pascal's triangle with coefficients $1,4,6,4,1$ (M1)

$2^{4}+4(2^{3})x+6(2^{2})x^{2}+4(2)x^{3}+x^{4}$ (A1)

$=16+32x+24x^{2}+8x^{3}+x^{4}$ A2

*Award A1 for 3 or 4 correct terms, A2 for all five terms correct.* [4]

text: Find the coefficient of $x^{7}$ in the expansion of $(2x-3)^{10}$. [4]
Find the constant term in the expansion of $\left(x^{2}+\dfrac{2}{x}\right)^{6}$. [5]
ms:
general term $\binom{6}{r}(x^{2})^{6-r}\left(\dfrac{2}{x}\right)^{r}$ (M1)

power of $x$: $12-2r-r=0$ (M1)

$r=4$ A1

$\binom{6}{4}(2)^{4}=15\times16$ (A1)

$=240$ A1 [5]

text:
In the expansion of $(1+kx)^{6}$, where $k>0$, the coefficient of $x^{2}$ is 135.

(a) Find the value of $k$. [3]

(b) Hence find the coefficient of $x^{3}$ in the expansion of $(2-x)(1+kx)^{6}$. [4]

The diagram shows the first seven rows of Pascal's triangle. Some of the numbers in the last row have been replaced by $p$, $q$ and $r$.

![Pascal's triangle rows 0 to 6, with the last row 1, 6, p, q, r, 6, 1](qbank/img/gen_math_SL1.9_5.svg)

(a) Write down the value of $p$, of $q$ and of $r$. [2]

(b) Hence find the coefficient of $x^{4}$ in the expansion of $(2x+3)^{6}$. [3]
ms:
**(a)** $p=15$, $q=20$, $r=15$ A2

*Award A1 for two correct values.* [2]

**(b)** $15\times(2x)^{4}\times3^{2}$ (M1)

$=15\times16\times9$ (A1)

$=2160$ A1

*Award (M1)(A1)A0 for $2160x^{4}$. FT from their $p$ or $r$.* [3]

text:
(a) Find the first three terms, in ascending powers of $x$, of the expansion of $\left(1+\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^{8}$. [3]

(b) By substituting a suitable value of $x$ into your answer to part (a), find an approximation for $1.005^{8}$. [2]

(c) Find the percentage error in using your answer to part (b) as an approximation for $1.005^{8}$. [2]
